procedural_history.originating_court: Complaint was registered with the police.
procedural_history.impugned_order: The appellants unsuccessfully sought the intervention of the High Court of Patna under Art. 226 of the Constitution in Cr. W.J.C. No. 11 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants filed a petition (Cr. W.J.C. No. 11 of 1966) in the High Court of Patna under Article 226 of the Constitution, seeking to stop the investigation against them. The High Court dismissed their petition on July 4, 1966.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave from the judgment and order of the Patna High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complaint made before the police disclosed a cognizable offence, thereby empowering the police to investigate the complaint.

facts: A complaint was registered with the police against the appellants, who were office bearers of a sugar company.
The complaint alleged that they failed to pay for sugarcane they had purchased within the prescribed time, which is an offense under the relevant law.
The appellants challenged the police's power to investigate, arguing that the complaint did not disclose a cognizable offense.
law: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr. P.C.), an offense is classified as cognizable based on its potential punishment.
According to Section 4(1)(f) and the 2nd Schedule of the Cr. P.C., an offense punishable with three years' imprisonment is a cognizable offense.
Police are empowered to investigate cognizable offenses without a court order.
application: The Court examined the punishment for the offense alleged in the complaint.
It found that the offense was punishable with three years' imprisonment.
Because the punishment was three years, the Court determined that the offense fell within the 2nd Schedule of the Cr. P.C.
Therefore, the Court concluded that the offense met the definition of a 'cognizable offence' under Section 4(1)(f) of the Cr. P.C.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' argument, holding that the complaint did disclose a cognizable offense because it was punishable with three years' imprisonment. As a result, the police were fully empowered to investigate the complaint.

issue.issue_text: Whether Parliament was competent to enact any law relating to the control of sugarcane, as the subject was contended to be within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State.

facts: The appellants argued that Parliament was not competent to pass a law controlling sugarcane.
Their reasoning was that sugarcane is part of 'agriculture', which is a subject within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State.
law: The Court referred to Entry 33 of List III (the Concurrent List) of the Constitution.
This entry empowers Parliament to legislate on the production, supply, and distribution of foodstuffs.
The Essential Commodities Act, passed by Parliament, defines 'essential commodity' to include 'foodstuffs' (Section 2(a)(v)) and further clarifies that 'food-crops include sugarcane' (Section 2(b)).
application: The Court reasoned that since sugarcane is classified as a food-crop and therefore a foodstuff under the Essential Commodities Act, it falls under the scope of Entry 33 of List III.
As Entry 33 is on the Concurrent List, Parliament has the power to legislate on this subject.
The Court also noted that Parliament had made the necessary declaration by law that it was expedient in the public interest to control foodstuffs.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' contention, holding that Parliament was well within its constitutional competence to enact the law controlling sugarcane by virtue of its power under Entry 33 of List III of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether the impugned order resulted in a violation of the fundamental right under Art. 19(1) of the Constitution.

facts: The appellants, office bearers of a sugar company, were being investigated for failing to pay sellers for sugarcane they had purchased within the time prescribed by the Sugarcane (Control) Order.
The appellants challenged this investigation, arguing that the order requiring them to pay within a specific time violated their fundamental right under Article 19(1) of the Constitution.
law: Article 19(1) of the Constitution guarantees certain fundamental rights to citizens.
application: The Court analyzed the nature of the right being asserted by the appellants.
It determined that the appellants were effectively claiming a fundamental right either not to pay the price for goods they had purchased, or to pay for them whenever they pleased.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' contention, holding that there is no fundamental right conferred on a buyer to refuse to pay the price of goods purchased or to pay for them at their own convenience. Therefore, the impugned order, which mandated timely payment, did not contravene Article 19(1).

issue.issue_text: Whether the contention that no cognizance could be taken of the offence in view of s. 11 of the Act was valid at the current stage of proceedings.

facts: A complaint was registered with the police against the appellants, who were office bearers of a sugar company.
The complaint was being investigated by the police.
The appellants objected to this investigation, raising several grounds, one of which was based on Section 11 of the Act.
application: The appellants contended that Section 11 of the Act prevented any cognizance from being taken of the alleged offence.
The Supreme Court observed that the case was still at the police investigation stage.
Crucially, the Court noted that no court had yet taken cognizance of the case.
Therefore, any argument about a legal bar to a court taking cognizance was not relevant at this point in the proceedings.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the contention, holding that the plea based on Section 11 of the Act was premature because the matter was still under investigation and no court had yet taken cognizance of the case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the power being exercised by the authorities was an implied one.

facts: The appellants argued that the power to regulate the price of sugarcane was an implied one, especially since the matter was expressly dealt with by the Bihar Sugar Factories Control Act, 1937.
law: Sub-rule (3) of rule 3 provides a specific mandate regarding the payment for sugarcane.
application: The Court found that sub-rule (3) of rule 3 specifically requires that unless there is a written agreement to the contrary, the purchaser must pay the seller the price of the sugarcane purchased within 14 days.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the contention that the power was an implied one, holding that it was explicitly and specifically provided for in sub-rule (3) of rule 3, which gives a specific mandate for payment.

cases.case_name: Ch. Tika Ramji & Ors. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.principle: Parliament has the competence under Entry 33 of List III of the Constitution to legislate in respect of the production, supply, and distribution of foodstuffs.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under the Constitution, Parliament is competent to legislate on the production, supply, and distribution of foodstuffs, a power which extends to food crops. A rule mandating payment for purchased goods within a specified period, absent a written agreement to the contrary, is a valid exercise of this power. Such a rule does not violate any fundamental right, as no such right exists to not pay for goods purchased. A pre-Constitution state law on the same subject can be altered or amended by a competent central legislature.
obiter: The question of whether cognizance of an offense could have been taken under section 11 of the Act is premature and does not arise in this case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the police investigation into the appellants' failure to pay for sugarcane was valid. It held that Parliament was competent to enact the Essential Commodities Act under its constitutional power to regulate foodstuffs, which includes sugarcane. The specific rule requiring timely payment was explicit, not implied, and did not violate any fundamental right, as there is no right to refuse payment for goods purchased. Therefore, the complaint disclosed a cognizable offence, and the appellants' challenge to the investigation was dismissed.
legal_tests_applied: Analysis of legislative competence under Entry 33 of List III of the Constitution.
Interpretation of statutory provisions to determine if a power is explicit or implied.
Assessment of whether a government order violates fundamental rights under Article 19(1) of the Constitution.
Analysis of the procedural stage of a criminal case to determine if a legal challenge is premature.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that Parliament lacked legislative competence, finding that Entry 33 of List III of the Constitution empowers Parliament to legislate on the production, supply, and distribution of foodstuffs, which includes sugarcane.

The contention that no cognizance could be taken of the offence under s. 11 of the Act was dismissed as premature because the case was still at the investigation stage and no court had yet taken cognizance.
The court found no substance in the claim that the order violated Article 19(1), stating that "No fundamentai right is conferred on a buyer not to pay the price of: the goods purchased by him".
The argument that the power being exercised was an implied one was incorrect, as the court found that "Sub-rule (3) of rule 3 specifically provides" for the obligation in question.
Because the underlying law and rules were held to be valid, the complaint alleging their violation was deemed to disclose a cognizable offence, thereby empowering the police to investigate.
why_respondent_won: Parliament's competence to enact the law was affirmed based on its power over foodstuffs under Entry 33 of List III of the Constitution.
The challenge regarding the court's ability to take cognizance was successfully countered as being premature, as the matter had not yet proceeded beyond the investigation phase.
The court agreed that the order did not violate any fundamental right, as the obligation to pay for goods is a basic commercial principle, not a restriction on fundamental freedoms.
The power to enforce payment was not implied but was explicitly provided for under Sub-rule (3) of rule 3, making the government's action lawful.
As the legal framework was valid, the complaint based on it was sufficient to initiate a police investigation into a cognizable offence.
policy_considerations: The court acknowledged the public policy behind the legislation, noting that Parliament had declared by law that "it is expedient in public interest that it should exercise control over foodstuffs."
The court implicitly upheld the policy of ensuring fair commercial dealings by stating that there is no fundamental right for a buyer to avoid paying the price for goods they have purchased.
